name: TPS7A0533PDBZR
title: TPS7A05 200 mA low-dropout regulator with 1 µA quiescent current, fixed 0.8 V to 3.3 V output
summary: The TPS7A05 is a family of fixed-output PMOS low-dropout regulators for loads up to 200 mA, drawing 1 µA typical (3 µA maximum) ground current and running from 1.4 V to 5.5 V input. It is aimed at battery equipment: lithium cells, Li-SOCl2 and Li-MnO2 primaries, or two and three alkaline cells. Outputs run from 0.8 V to 3.3 V with 1% typical accuracy; it is stable with 0.47 µF or more on the output and has foldback current limit, thermal shutdown, undervoltage lockout and, on P versions, a 120 Ω output discharge. TPS7A0533PDBZR is the 3.3 V version with discharge in the 3-pin SOT-23 (DBZ), which has no enable pin, on a 3000-piece reel.

operation.text: Three features speed the loop without raising the steady quiescent current. Dynamic biasing raises IQ for a short time during a transient, widening the loop bandwidth. Adaptive biasing raises IQ as the DC load grows. A buffered reference holds the loop at unity gain whatever the output voltage, so the response time is the same across the output range.

P versions switch a 120 Ω resistor from OUT to ground through an internal MOSFET whenever the part is disabled, in undervoltage lockout or in thermal shutdown. The output then decays with the time constant of COUT against 120 Ω in parallel with the load. The discharge path is not meant for draining a large output capacitance after the input has collapsed: current can then flow backwards from OUT to IN and damage the part. Reverse current is to be held to no more than 5% of the rated current.
The part senses when it is in dropout and switches the adaptive biasing off, so IQ rises only a little in dropout.

The output stays off until VIN rises past the UVLO rising threshold (1.3 V typical) and turns off again when VIN falls below the falling threshold (rising threshold less about 40 mV of hysteresis). In lockout, P versions pull OUT to ground through 120 Ω. A brownout that stays above the falling threshold leaves the part enabled, though the output can drop out of regulation; one that goes below it disables the part in most cases, the output falls under the load and the discharge resistor, and the part starts up normally once VIN climbs back over the rising threshold.

EN is active high: above VEN(HI) (0.9 V min) the output is on, below VEN(LO) (0.4 V max) the output is off and every internal circuit is shut down. Holding EN below VEN(LO) before the next turn-on gives a normal start-up with the controlled ramp, provided the output capacitor has had time to discharge. Where no shutdown is needed, EN is connected to IN; VEN may not exceed VIN. The DBZ package has no EN pin.

The current limit falls as the output voltage falls. With VOUT at 90% of nominal the limit is ICL (450 mA typical); with OUT forced to 0 V it is ISC (65 mA typical). Above about 500 mV of output the limit acts as a brick wall at ICL, so the part starts normally into constant-current loads and into a negatively biased output. Below about 1 mA of load the foldback circuit is switched off to save IQ, so the limit responds more slowly to a fault that starts from a light load. High dissipation in current limit can trip thermal shutdown. Inductance in the input and load wiring is kept small so the limit works properly; continuous current-limit operation is not recommended.

The part turns off when the pass transistor's junction reaches Tsd(Shutdown) (160 °C typical) and turns back on when it has cooled to Tsd(Reset) (140 °C typical). Because the die heats and cools quickly, the output can cycle on and off until the dissipation is lowered. The junction is kept at or below 125 °C: above it the part leaves its specifications, and running repeatedly into shutdown or above 125 °C shortens its life. A fast start-up while TJ is above Tsd(Reset) makes shutdown assert at Tsd(Reset), and the part stays off until the junction is below Tsd(Shutdown). The protection is no replacement for heat sinking.

Normal: the output is regulated to its nominal value. Dropout: the input is too low for regulation, the pass transistor acts as a resistor, VOUT is VIN less VDO, and PSRR, noise and transient response are much worse. Disabled: the pass transistor and all internal circuitry are off, and an internal resistor pulls the output down to ground.

The part is stable with low-ESR ceramic capacitors on input and output. X7R, X5R and C0G dielectrics hold their value fairly well over temperature; Y5V is discouraged for its large capacitance change. Any ceramic loses effective capacitance with bias voltage and temperature, possibly down to half its nominal value; the recommended input and output values already assume about 50% of nominal remains.

No input capacitor is needed for stability, but one from IN to GND is good practice: it offsets a reactive source and gives better PSRR, less input ripple and a better transient response. It is recommended when the source impedance is above 0.5 Ω, and a larger one may be needed for large, fast load or line steps or when the part sits several inches from its supply. An output capacitor within the recommended range (0.47 µF to 22 µF) is needed for stability and improves dynamic performance.

Below 15 °C ambient, IN is ramped down over no less than 10 ms and EN over no less than 100 µs when powering down. A faster IN ramp-down can make the next power-up a partial start, a shut-off and then a normal soft start. A faster EN ramp-down can delay the next start by up to 130 ms before a normal soft start. A fast ramp-down charges high-impedance nodes inside the part, which take a long time to discharge below 15 °C.

On a light-to-heavy step the output first dips as the output capacitor's charge is drawn out through its parasitic impedance, then recovers as the regulator raises its current. On a heavy-to-light step it first rises because the regulator is still sourcing a large current into the output capacitor, then recovers as the regulator cuts its current and the load drains the capacitor. More output capacitance lowers the peaks but slows the response; a higher DC load also lowers the peaks, since the step is smaller and the capacitor has a stronger discharge path.

The pass element is a PMOS transistor. When VIN – VOUT is below VDO it works in its linear region, and IN to OUT looks like its drain-source resistance, so VDO grows with output current and varies with temperature. PSRR and transient response worsen as the input-output difference approaches dropout.

A load step can pull a high-ESR battery supply down into dropout; one case is two 1.55 V coin cells with 30 Ω ESR making a 2.5 V rail, where a step from 1 µA to 25 mA sags the input by 750 mV. With the pass element driven fully on, the error amplifier saturates and must recover before the pass element returns to active mode, so VOUT overshoots in the meantime. A loop pulldown circuit inside reduces the overshoot; a higher DC load or more output capacitance reduces it further by giving the excess charge somewhere to go.

Because the error amplifier responds slowly in dropout, a line step while in dropout can move the output by much more than in regulation, and the deviation can exceed twice the regulated output voltage.

Other heat sources are kept away from the regulator on the board. Choosing the input rail close to the output keeps dissipation down. RθJA depends strongly on copper area, copper weight and plane placement; the RθJA in the thermal table comes from a JEDEC test board and only compares packages. With a good thermal layout, RθJA of the DQN package amounts to its RθJC(bot) added to what the board copper contributes.

The ΨJT and ΨJB metrics estimate the junction temperature in circuit on a typical board and depend little on copper area. They are not true thermal resistances. TJ is found from the package-top temperature with ΨJT, or from the board temperature beside the package with ΨJB.

The continuous operating area is bounded by dropout (minimum VIN – VOUT at a given current), by the rated output current, by the rated junction temperature (a curve in which allowed current falls as VIN – VOUT rises, from the IOUT equation) and by the input voltage range, which limits both the minimum and the maximum VIN – VOUT.

Input range 1.4 V to 5.5 V, from a well-regulated, low-noise supply. For regulation and best dynamic performance the input is at least VOUT(nom) + 0.5 V. An input capacitor of 1 µF or more lowers the supply impedance, especially during transients.

Input and output capacitors sit as close to the part as possible. Copper planes on the device connections and thermal vias around the part spread heat. No thermal via goes directly under the DQN thermal pad, since a via can draw solder away from the pad joint during reflow. CIN sits next to IN and COUT next to OUT, and GND joins a ground plane.

Fixed outputs are ordered by code in the part number. Outputs from 1.0 V to 3.3 V in 50 mV steps can be made through the factory. The P in the part number marks versions with active output discharge; TPS7A0518YKAR has none.

Body sizes of the SOT-23 packages exclude mold flash, protrusions and gate burrs, which are at most 0.25 mm per side. DBV follows JEDEC MO-178; DBZ follows JEDEC TO-236 apart from its minimum foot length. On the DQN the thermal pad is soldered to the board for thermal and mechanical performance.
